title: Section check: Geography & Our Environment
intro: 10 questions about Lessons 10–14. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: Long ago, why did towns often grow at places where boats stopped on a river?

options.text: Boats kept the river from flooding
options.feedback: Not quite. Boats cannot stop a river from flooding. Towns grew where boats stopped because people could trade there. Look back at Lesson 10.
Yes. Boats carried heavy goods, like grain and wood. People bought and sold these goods where the boats stopped.

options.text: The land was high and rocky
options.feedback: Not quite. Boats stop by the water, not on high, rocky land. Look back at Lesson 10.

stimulus.title: Notes from the made-up Riverlands map in Lesson 10
items: River site: flat land by the river. The soil is good for crops. Sometimes the river floods it.
Hill site: high, dry ground. Floods do not reach it. The soil is thin and rocky.
Forest site: far from the river. There is wood to build with. People must cut trees before they farm.

questions.question: Which fact is a good reason to build a farming town at the River site?

options.text: The soil there is good for crops.
options.feedback: Yes. The map says the soil at the River site is good for crops. Mud from the river makes the land fertile.
Not quite. Floods do not reach the Hill site. But the river sometimes floods the River site. Look back at Lesson 10.

options.text: There is wood to build with there.
options.feedback: Not quite. The wood is at the Forest site. The River site is flat land next to the river. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.question: Which part of a map tells you what each colour, line and shape means?

options.feedback: Not quite. The scale helps you see how far things are in real life. Look back at Lesson 11.
Not quite. The compass rose shows north, south, east and west. Look back at Lesson 11.
Yes. The key, or legend, tells you what each symbol means. For example, a blue line can stand for a river.

stimulus.title: A made-up map of Ambrey Park
items: The path from the gate to the pond is five squares long.
Compass rose: N (north) points to the top of the map

questions.question: About how long is the path from the gate to the pond?

options.feedback: Not quite. The path is five squares long, and each square is 10 metres. Look back at Lesson 11.
Yes. Each square is 10 metres. Five squares make 50 metres.
Not quite. That would be 50 squares. The path is only five squares of 10 metres each. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.question: Nairobi and Shenzhen are two real cities. What helped both of them grow?

options.text: Cool weather and lots of rain
options.feedback: Not quite. Weather did not make these two cities grow. Nairobi began as a stop on a railway, and Shenzhen grew when factories opened. Look back at Lesson 12.
Not quite. Rich soil helps farms grow crops. These two cities grew because of jobs and transport. Look back at Lesson 12.
Yes. Nairobi began as a stop on a railway, and factories opened in Shenzhen. Jobs and transport brought many people.

stimulus.title: A made-up town: Ostrin
stimulus.body: A new train line opens in the made-up town of Ostrin. A factory opens next to the station, with 600 new jobs. Five years later, twice as many people live in Ostrin. But the town still has only one small school.

questions.question: What problem is Ostrin most likely to have?

options.text: The one school gets very crowded.
options.feedback: Yes. The number of people grew fast, but the school did not. A service needs to grow when the population grows.

options.text: There are fewer jobs in the town.
options.feedback: Not quite. The factory brought 600 new jobs, so there are more jobs, not fewer. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: It is hard to get to other towns.
options.feedback: Not quite. The new train line makes travel easier. Think about the school instead. Look back at Lesson 12.

stimulus.title: A made-up town: Kelmar
stimulus.body: Kelmar is a made-up town. For the last 40 years, its summers have been hot and dry. Most of its rain has fallen in winter. Today, a cool wind is blowing, and grey clouds cover the sky.

questions.question: Which one is about weather, not climate?

options.text: Summers are usually hot and dry.
options.feedback: Not quite. This is a pattern over many years, so it is climate. Weather is what the air is like now. Look back at Lesson 13.

options.text: A cool wind is blowing today.
options.feedback: Yes. This is about one day, and it can change fast. That makes it weather.
Not quite. This is what usually happens each year, so it is climate. Weather is what the air is like now. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.question: What are the seasons like near the equator?

options.feedback: Not quite. Many places far from the equator have these four seasons. Look back at Lesson 13.
Not quite. Places near the equator are warm all year. Look back at Lesson 13.

options.text: A rainy season and a dry season
options.feedback: Yes. Near the equator, it is warm all year. So the seasons are usually rainy or dry.

stimulus.title: The made-up town of Brookside from Lesson 14: three ideas for a low bridge
items: The problem: heavy rain sometimes covers the low footbridge with water.
Idea A: put a warning sign by the bridge. It is cheap and quick.
Idea B: build the bridge higher and add a ramp. It costs more and takes months.
Idea C: send phone messages and put up paper notices when heavy rain is coming.

questions.question: What is one problem with Idea A, the warning sign?

options.text: It does not make the bridge safer.
options.feedback: Yes. A sign is quick and cheap, but the bridge stays low. Also, some people cannot read the sign.

options.text: It costs a lot and takes months.
options.feedback: Not quite. That is Idea B, raising the bridge. A sign is cheap and quick. Look back at Lesson 14.

options.text: Everyone needs a phone to see it.
options.feedback: Not quite. Phone messages are part of Idea C. A sign stands by the bridge, so no phone is needed. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.question: A made-up library puts its signs in three languages and adds pictures. Now everyone can find what they need. What is this an example of?

options.feedback: Not quite. An alert is a message that warns people about danger. These signs help people find things. Look back at Lesson 14.
Not quite. The environment is the land, water, air, plants and animals around us. Look back at Lesson 14.
Yes. Inclusion means making sure everyone can take part. Signs in three languages, with pictures, help more people.

results.high: Well done. You know a lot about places, maps and how people live with their environment.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 10–14, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
